result.summary: Pausanias describes the sanctuary of Aesculapius at Epidaurus: its rules, the cult statue, paintings, healing pillars and Polycletus's theatre. He also records the Hippolytus tradition at Aricia and the buildings added by the senator Antonine.

scenes.title: The grove, statue and Rotunda
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the walled grove, its rules, the ivory and gold statue and the paintings of Pausias in the Rotunda.

scenes.title: Healing pillars and Hippolytus
scenes.summary: The pillars record cures, and one records Hippolytus's horses. The Aricians say Æsculapius revived him and he became king in Italy.
scenes.stakes: Hippolytus has died through his father's curse and is restored to life.

scenes.title: Theatre and Antonine's buildings
scenes.summary: Pausanias praises Polycletus's theatre, lists other buildings in the grove, and the works of Antonine, including the sanctuary on Mount Cynortion.

alias_notes.explanation: Apollo under a local cult title at Mount Cynortion.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias ranks theatres and praises Polycletus's sense of proportion.

analysis.text: The passage shows Epidaurus as a healing sanctuary, with ritual purity rules and recorded cures.
Antonine's restorations show Roman patrons maintaining Greek sanctuaries in Pausanias's time.

fun_facts.text: The theatre of Epidaurus is still used for performances and is famed for its acoustics.

language_notes.text: Delos, Apollo's sacred island, was ritually purified so that no one was allowed to be born or die there.
Titane was a place in Sicyonia with a sanctuary of Æsculapius, mentioned earlier in Pausanias.
Pausias was a celebrated painter of Sicyon, in the fourth century BC, known for encaustic work and for his paintings of Cupid.
Doric is the Greek dialect spoken in Epidaurus and much of the Peloponnese.
Hippolytus was cursed by his father Theseus after a false accusation by Phaedra; Aricia was a town in Latium with a cult of Artemis.
Senator here means a Roman senator; Pausanias names him only as Antonine, a benefactor of Epidaurus.
Porch means a colonnade or portico, not a small entrance.
Reservoir translates a cistern built to catch rainwater.

context_notes.text: The Olympian Zeus at Athens was the huge temple statue of Zeus, so this Æsculapius is large, though half its size.
The staff, serpent and dog are Æsculapius's usual attributes; he was the god of healing.
Suppliants slept in the sanctuary hoping the god would send healing dreams or cures.
This is probably the younger Polycletus, an architect of the fourth century BC; the famous sculptor was an earlier man.
Epione was the wife of Æsculapius in cult, and Hygiea was his daughter, a goddess of health.

literary_notes.text: The reflected woman's face in the glass bowl is a vivid visual detail showing Pausias's skill.
Pausanias ends a ranked comparison of theatres with a question, stressing that Polycletus's work is unrivalled in harmony.
The building where it is lawful both to die and bear children contrasts the earlier taboo, and gently marks Antonine's practical remedy.
